core_obligations: Choose a decreasing countable fundamental system of open submodules of M, note that its images form a fundamental system in the quotient, and reduce completeness of the quotient to the identity expressing it as an inverse limit (proof lines 980-986).

Write the short exact sequences relating the quotients and use surjectivity of the transition maps of the system of quotients of N to conclude from the exactness statement that the completion of M surjects onto the limit (proof lines 986-991).
Identify the kernel of that surjection as N using that N is closed, and record that the quotient map is open by definition of the quotient topology (proof lines 991-995).
proof_roadmap: Fundamental systems and the reduction to an inverse limit (proof lines 980-986).
The short exact sequences and the surjection from the completion (proof lines 986-991).
The kernel, and openness of the quotient map (proof lines 991-995).
difficulty_reason: For a closed submodule N of a complete linearly topologized module M with a countable fundamental system of neighbourhoods of zero, the lemma asserts that the quotient is complete and that the quotient map is open (statement lines 971-978). The proof chooses a decreasing countable fundamental system of open submodules, observes that its images form a fundamental system in the quotient, and so reduces completeness of the quotient to the identity expressing it as the inverse limit of the quotients by the images (proof lines 980-986). It then writes the evident short exact sequences relating the quotients of M, of N and of the quotient module; since the transition maps of the system of quotients of N are surjective, the exactness statement for inverse limits applies and shows that the completion of M, which is M by hypothesis, surjects onto that limit (proof lines 986-991). The kernel of the resulting map is identified as N because N is closed, and the openness of the quotient map is the definition of the quotient topology (proof lines 991-995). The claim is H2: the reduction to an inverse limit, the application of the exactness statement using surjectivity of the transition maps, and the identification of the kernel are each displayed.
